rows.vgi.doc_llm: The current top of book for ONE OUTCOME TOKEN, in a single row: best bid, best ask, midpoint and spread. Takes a `token_id` from a market's `outcomes` list. This is the cheapest way to ask 'what is this outcome trading at right now' — prefer it over `orderbook()` when you do not need depth, and over the price columns on `markets()` when you need the number to be live rather than as of Gamma's last refresh.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
One row per token, assembled from the CLOB's batched quote endpoints.

### Midpoint is the number you usually want — if the spread is tight

`midpoint` sits halfway between best bid and best ask and is what Polymarket displays as the price. Because a share pays $1 if its outcome happens, it reads as an implied probability: 0.62 is 62%.

**Check `spread` before believing it.** A midpoint is only a forecast to the extent that someone is willing to trade near it. On a thin market the two sides can be almost unrelated — a real book quoted 0.020 bid against 0.990 ask, whose midpoint of 0.505 is not a coin flip but the average of two numbers nobody would trade at. That is why this function returns `spread` alongside `midpoint` rather than only the price: a wide spread means the number above it is noise, and `orderbook()` will show how little is resting behind it.

### Naming

The CLOB reports quotes as `BUY` and `SELL`, and the mapping is the opposite of the obvious one: `BUY` is the best **bid** and `SELL` is the best **ask**, verified against the raw book. They are renamed here to the side of the book they actually sit on, so `best_ask >= best_bid` always holds and `spread` is never negative.

### Cost under LATERAL

Two batched requests per 200 tokens regardless of how many rows drive it, so a quote across a whole topic is cheap.

### Freshness

The CLOB declares no cacheability on quotes, so nothing here is cached. That is the honest policy for a top-of-book read: the number is only worth having if it is current.

How one outcome's price moved over time, as a sampled series

rows.vgi.doc_llm: The historical price series for ONE OUTCOME TOKEN — the time-series view. Reach for it to chart or backtest how an outcome's implied probability moved, rather than where it stands now. Takes a `token_id` from a market's `outcomes` list. Passing a condition id instead returns an EMPTY SERIES with no error, so an empty result usually means the wrong identifier rather than an untraded market.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
A sampled price curve for one outcome token.

### It takes a token id, and the failure is silent

The underlying parameter is called `market`, but it wants a **token id**. A condition id is answered with HTTP 200 and an empty history — indistinguishable from an outcome that never traded. Get the token from `unnest(markets.outcomes)`.

### Not OHLC

Polymarket publishes one price per sampled instant, so each row is a single `price` rather than a bar. `fidelity` is the gap between samples in minutes; `period` is how far back to look.

### Window and caching

Every call ends at the present and requires both `period` and `fidelity`. The series therefore contains a still-forming final point and follows the origin's 90-second cache lifetime. Explicit start/end windows are not part of the SQL surface.

Repeated observations with the same timestamp and exact numeric price within one response are returned once, preserving their first position. Conflicting prices at the same timestamp raise an error; the worker does not choose one. This normalization is local to each token response, without merging separate calls or rounding prices.

### Prices are probabilities

Each `price` is USDC per share between 0 and 1, so the curve reads as the market's implied probability over time. These are traded prices rather than a normalised display figure, so a flat stretch means nothing traded — not that the market held an opinion steady. Pair it with `quote()` if you need to know whether there is a market behind the curve right now.

Every open position one wallet holds, with its profit and loss

rows.vgi.doc_llm: Every open position one wallet holds, with entry price, current value and unrealised P&L. Takes a wallet address — a THIRD key, distinct from both market identifiers — which you get from `holders()` or from the trader columns on `trades()`. This is the reverse of `holders()`: that answers 'who is in this market', this answers 'what else is this person in'. Reach for it to follow a large or successful trader across the whole site.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
One row per open position, keyed on the holder's wallet.

### The third key

This is the only function here keyed on a wallet address rather than on a market or an outcome. Get one from `holders()` (who is in this market) or from the `proxy_wallet` column of `trades()` (who just traded).

### Closing the loop

`holders()` goes market to wallet; this goes wallet to market. Chaining them is how you get from 'this market moved' to 'here is who moved it and what else they hold' — which is possible only because Polymarket settles on a public chain.

### Reading the P&L

`cash_pnl` is unrealised profit in USDC and `percent_pnl` is the same as a percentage — a percentage, not a fraction, so -44.5 means down 44.5%. `avg_price` against `cur_price` gives the direction directly, and both are probabilities between 0 and 1. `redeemable` marks a resolved market whose position can be cashed out.

### Cross-API lifecycle

The Data API can retain a position after Gamma retires its catalog record. In that case the row remains valid here, but passing its `condition_id` to `market()` returns no row; use the denormalised `title` and `event_slug` carried by the position itself.

### Freshness

Polymarket declares `max-age=5` here, the shortest TTL it publishes anywhere, because a position's value moves with the market price.

rows.vgi.doc_llm: A single market's current snapshot, by exact condition id. Use this when you already have a condition id — from a trade row, say — and want the question behind it; use `markets()` when you want to browse or filter. Same columns as `markets()`, so the two are interchangeable downstream, and unlike `markets()` this composes under a correlated LATERAL.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
One row for one market, looked up by `condition_id`.

### When to use this instead of `markets()`

`markets()` is the browse path and streams a catalog; this is the point lookup, and it is the one that works as the inner side of a `LATERAL`. It is the natural way back from a trade or a holding to the question being traded.

### Cost

Requests are batched behind the scenes: Gamma accepts up to 60 condition ids per call, so a join over hundreds of markets costs a handful of requests, not hundreds.

### An unknown id returns nothing

Gamma answers a filter that matches nothing with an empty list rather than a 404, so a condition id that does not exist produces no rows — the same as one that does exist but was filtered away.

Resting order-book depth for one outcome, one row per side and price level

rows.vgi.doc_llm: Resting order-book depth for ONE OUTCOME TOKEN, flattened to one row per side and price level so it aggregates and joins like an ordinary table. Takes a `token_id` from a market's `outcomes` list — NOT a condition id, which is a 404 here. Reach for this to see liquidity behind the best quote: spread, depth at a price, or the shape of one side. For just the top of book use `quote()`, which is one row instead of many.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
The CLOB returns a book as nested `bids` and `asks`; this flattens it to one row per (side, price level).

### It takes a token id

Each outcome of a market trades as its own token with its own book. Get the `token_id` from `unnest(markets.outcomes)`. A condition id here is an HTTP 404 — which at least fails loudly, unlike `price_history()`, where the same mistake returns an empty series.

### Reading the two sides

`bid` rows are buyers, `ask` rows are sellers, and the outcomes of a binary market mirror each other: a Yes bid at 0.40 is economically a No ask at 0.60. There is no `depth` argument: the batched endpoint returns the whole book either way, and SQL caps it exactly — `QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY side ORDER BY CASE WHEN side = 'bid' THEN -price ELSE price END) <= 5`. The side-aware ordering matters: best bids are highest, while best asks are lowest.

### Cost under LATERAL

Books are fetched in batches of up to 200 tokens per request, which is what makes a join across a whole topic affordable: measured at 12.85s for 100 books individually against 0.16s batched. No query change is needed; it happens automatically.

### An empty result

A token with no resting orders contributes no rows, and so does a token the batch endpoint omits — both mean 'nothing is resting here'.

rows.vgi.doc_llm: The entry point to Polymarket's market data: one row per tradeable question, with its current price, volume and lifecycle state. Reach for this to browse or filter — start from a `tag_id` out of the `tags` table, or pass `order_by => 'volume24hr'` to see what is busy right now. The `outcomes` column is the important one: it carries each outcome's `token_id`, which is what `orderbook()`, `quote()` and `price_history()` key on. The `condition_id` column is a DIFFERENT key, and is what `trades()` and `holders()` take. Passing one where the other belongs usually returns an empty result rather than an error.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
Markets are the tradeable questions on Polymarket. Each has two or more outcomes, and each outcome trades as its own CLOB token.

### The two identifiers

This is the thing to get right, because getting it wrong is usually silent:

- `condition_id` (`0x` + 64 hex) identifies the **market**. `trades()` and `holders()` take it.
- `token_id` (a long decimal string, inside `outcomes`) identifies **one outcome**. `orderbook()`, `quote()` and `price_history()` take it.

Both are called `market` in Polymarket's own URLs, which is where the confusion comes from.

### Reading `outcomes`

Polymarket sends outcome names, prices and token ids as three separate JSON-encoded strings whose only relationship is positional. They are zipped here into one list of structs so the correspondence cannot be got wrong. Reach the individual outcomes by unnesting that column in a LATERAL — the shipped example queries show the exact form, which needs `recursive := true` to expose the struct's fields as columns.

### Prices are probabilities, where the market is liquid

Every price column is USDC per share between 0 and 1, and a share pays $1 if its outcome happens — so a price of 0.62 reads as a 62% implied probability. They are `DECIMAL`, never `DOUBLE`.

The prices inside `outcomes` are Polymarket's displayed figures, normalised to sum to 1 across a market's outcomes. That means they always *look* like a coherent forecast, even when nothing is resting on the book. Before treating one as a probability, check the real quote: `quote()` returns the `spread` and `orderbook()` the size behind it. A market quoting 0.02 bid against 0.99 ask has a displayed price and no market.

### Streaming

Rows arrive one API page at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops early instead of paying for the whole catalog. The cost is that this cannot be the inner side of a correlated `LATERAL` — drive a join from it, not into it. Use `market()` for the per-row lookup.

rows.vgi.doc_md:
One row per execution, with the trader attached.

### It takes a condition id

This is the Data API, which keys on the market rather than the outcome. A token id is rejected with HTTP 400 (`invalid condition id`). Each row's `token_id` column tells you which outcome changed hands.

### Public counterparties

`proxy_wallet`, `trader_name` and `pseudonym` identify the taker. This is ordinary public chain data, and it is what makes flow analysis possible here in a way it is not on a conventional exchange.

### Volume

An active market can have a very long tape, which is why `max_rows` is required rather than defaulted — the call should say how much it wants, up to 10,000 trades per call.

### Prices arrive as floats

The Data API sends price and size as JSON numbers rather than strings. They are recovered to exact `DECIMAL` through the shortest round-tripping representation, so a 0.955 print reads as 0.955 and not as 0.9549999999.

An event groups the markets that resolve together. A single-question event has one market under it; an election event has one per candidate.

`tags` is a list of `{tag_id, label, slug}` structs — flattening it would fan every event out into one row per tag. `unnest` the column when you do want that shape.

Gamma sends event-level volume and liquidity as JSON numbers where the market level sends the same quantities as strings. Both are carried to `DECIMAL` through the same converter, so the two levels compare exactly.

### Paging

Rows stream a page at a time, so a `LIMIT` stops early. Gamma clamps the page size to 100 silently rather than erroring on a larger request.

One row per holder per outcome, ranked by size.

### Why this exists at all

Positions are on-chain, so the holder list is public data rather than something an exchange chooses to publish. There is no equivalent on Kalshi or a conventional venue.

### Shape

The API groups holders under each outcome token; that grouping is flattened here and the `token_id` stamped onto every row, so a holder row can say which side of the question it is a position in. `amount` is shares of that outcome, and each share pays $1 if the outcome happens.

Summing `amount` by `token_id` and comparing the top holder to the rest is the usual way to ask whether a price is one whale's opinion or a crowd's.

Displayed-book fill price and slippage for a given order size, before fees

rows.vgi.doc_llm: The price a given order size would actually get, having consumed the resting book level by level. Takes a `token_id`, a side, and a share count. Reach for this instead of `quote()` whenever size matters: a market can quote a one-tick spread and hold fifteen shares behind it, so the midpoint is a real price at which almost nothing trades. `avg_price` is what the position costs per share, `slippage` is what the size cost over the touch, and `fully_filled` says whether the book could cover the request at all. Values are pre-fee: this function models displayed liquidity, not venue fees.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
One row per request, computed from the same batched book `orderbook()` returns — so it costs no extra call when driven alongside it.

### Why the touch is not enough

Spread measures the distance between the best bid and the best ask. It says nothing about how much is standing there. A live market quoted a 0.001 spread on 15 shares; another quoted 0.97 on a book with one order a side. Neither number tells you what a position would cost, and this does.

### Reading the result

`avg_price` is size-weighted across every level consumed. `slippage` is the distance from the touch, signed so that it is always the cost of size rather than a direction — never negative. `fully_filled = false` means the book ran out: the row prices the portion that could fill, and the rest of the order would move the price further than this reports. `notional` and `avg_price` are computed from displayed book levels before any applicable venue fees.

### Sizing a strategy

Comparing `avg_price` across candidates at the size you actually intend to trade is a different ranking from comparing midpoints, and it is the one that survives contact with the book.

Every Polymarket series (the scan backing the `series` table)

rows.vgi.doc_llm: Every recurring question series on Polymarket, as a function. Prefer the `series` table, which scans this. A series is a question that opens a new event each occurrence — 'NFL' opens one per game — so this is the level to start from for anything periodic. Take a `slug` and pass it to `events()` as `series_slug`. Note that most one-off markets belong to no series at all, so this is a view of the recurring part of the site rather than of all of it.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
Polymarket's recurring question series — about 2,400 rows, streamed a page at a time.

### Prefer the table

The `series` catalog table is backed by this function and reads as plain SQL. This function returns exactly the same rows; the `all_` prefix exists only so that the function and the table can coexist in one schema.

### What a series is, and is not

A series groups events that recur: `nfl` opens an event per game, and each of those events carries a market per outcome. Plenty of Polymarket's biggest markets are one-offs that belong to no series, so this does **not** enumerate the site — `tags` is the axis that covers everything.

### Cost

Each series inlines every event beneath it, and those events inline their markets: 50 series come to 1.73 MB with the events and 31.6 KB without. This scan asks Gamma to exclude them, which is the difference between ~83 MB and ~1.5 MB for the whole catalog.

One wallet's history of trades, redemptions, yield and rebates

rows.vgi.doc_llm: Everything one wallet has done, newest first — the history counterpart to `positions()`, which reports only what it holds now. Takes a wallet address, the same key `positions()` takes. Reach for it to reconstruct how a trader built a position, or when they got out. Note the feed is broader than a trade tape: on a long-lived wallet most entries are `YIELD` accruals, so filter on `activity_type = 'TRADE'` when you want executions.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
One row per event in a wallet's history.

### Wider than a trade tape

`activity_type` distinguishes `TRADE` from `REDEEM` (cashing out a resolved market), `YIELD` (interest accrued on collateral), `MAKER_REBATE` and `TAKER_REBATE`, and the `SPLIT`/`MERGE` operations that convert between a dollar and a full set of outcome shares. Only `TRADE` rows carry a price and a side; the rest leave those NULL rather than reporting a misleading zero. Across a sample of active wallets, trades were roughly 92% of all entries.

### Completing the chain

`holders()` goes market to wallet, `positions()` goes wallet to its current markets, and this goes wallet to everything it has ever done. All three are public because Polymarket settles on a public chain.

### Volume

An active wallet has a very long history, so `max_rows` is required and capped at 5,000 entries per call.

Find events by searching their text, the way the site's search box does

rows.vgi.doc_llm: Full-text search over events — the way in when you know the subject but not the tag or the slug. Reach for this FIRST for any question phrased in words ('markets about the Fed', 'anything on Bitcoin'), because no other object here searches text: filtering `markets()` on a title predicate downloads the whole catalog to do it. Returns the same columns `events()` does, so chain it into `event_markets()` to reach the tradeable questions.
rows.vgi.doc_md:
Gamma's search endpoint, returning events with the same columns `events()` gives.

### Why this exists

It is the only text search in the catalog. Gamma's other filters match ids, slugs and tags — never free text — so a `WHERE title ILIKE '%bitcoin%'` on `events()` cannot be pushed down and pages the entire catalog over the network to filter locally. This asks the search index instead.

### Where to go next

Take an `event_id` and pass it to `event_markets()` for the markets beneath, then unnest their outcomes to reach prices and books.

### Paging

Results stream a page at a time and are ranked by relevance, so a `LIMIT` takes the best matches rather than an arbitrary slice.
